title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 2
text: The Patents Act defines an invention as a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 3
text: Section 3 lists subject matter that is not treated as an invention under the Indian Patents Act, including specified exclusions relevant to patentability.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 3
text: Section 3(p) excludes an invention which in effect is traditional knowledge, or an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component or components.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 3
text: Section 3(d) addresses certain new forms or new uses of known substances and sets conditions under which such subject matter is not treated as an invention.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 3
text: Section 3(i) excludes specified methods of medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic or therapeutic treatment.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 8
text: Applicants prosecuting the same or substantially the same invention abroad must provide prescribed information and an undertaking regarding foreign applications.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 10
text: A complete specification must fully and particularly describe the invention, disclose the best method known to the applicant, and end with claims defining the scope of protection.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 25
text: Section 25 provides opposition grounds including lack of novelty, lack of inventive step, insufficient disclosure, and certain disclosure failures involving biological material and traditional knowledge.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 64
text: Section 64 lists grounds for revocation including lack of novelty, lack of inventive step, insufficient disclosure, and anticipation based on knowledge available within a local or indigenous community.

title: Patents Rules, 2003 — Official Rules Resource
text: IP India publishes the Patents Rules, 2003 and amendment materials through its official patent rules resources.

title: 35 U.S.C. § 101 — Patentable Subject Matter
text: USPTO guidance explains that eligible patent subject matter includes processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter, subject to judicial exceptions.

title: 35 U.S.C. § 102 — Novelty
text: U.S. patent law includes novelty requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 102, with patentability affected by qualifying prior-art disclosures.

title: 35 U.S.C. § 103 — Non-Obviousness
text: USPTO guidance explains that a claimed invention may be unpatentable when differences from prior art would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art.

title: 35 U.S.C. § 112 — Specification and Claims
text: U.S. patent law requires a specification that supports the claimed invention, with requirements addressing description, enablement, and claims.

title: Patents Act 1977 — Section 1: Patentable Inventions
text: UK patentability under Section 1 requires an invention to be new, involve an inventive step, be capable of industrial application, and not fall within statutory exclusions.

title: Patents Act 1977 — Section 2: Novelty
text: Under UK Section 2, an invention is new when it does not form part of the state of the art before the relevant priority date.

title: Patents Act 1977 — Section 3: Inventive Step
text: Under UK Section 3, an invention involves an inventive step when it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art, having regard to the state of the art.

title: Patents Act 1977 — Section 4: Industrial Application
text: Under UK Section 4, an invention has industrial application when it can be made or used in any kind of industry, including agriculture.

title: Patent Cooperation Treaty — Introduction
text: The PCT provides an international filing system allowing an applicant to seek patent protection in multiple Contracting States through one international application.

title: PCT — International Patent System
text: WIPO provides PCT legal texts, the PCT Applicant's Guide, forms, official notices, fees information and other resources for international patent filing.

title: Traditional Knowledge and Intellectual Property
text: WIPO provides resources on intellectual property and traditional knowledge, including traditional medical knowledge, documentation, and defensive protection.

title: Patent Disclosure Requirements for Genetic Resources and Traditional Knowledge
text: WIPO maintains an up-to-date resource of national legislative and administrative measures on disclosure requirements related to genetic resources and traditional knowledge.

This document is a synthetic test source for the IP-SAKTI Sahayak knowledge-base ingestion
and retrieval workflow.

preparation.
Formulation
The formulation contains Ashwagandha root extract, Brahmi leaf extract, and Turmeric
rhizome extract.
The ingredients are combined in a fixed proportion and prepared as a standardized oral
herbal formulation.
Processing
The botanical ingredients are cleaned, dried, powdered, and extracted.
The extracts are filtered and blended before final formulation.
The process is intended to maintain consistent composition between batches.

The formulation is described for general wellness support in this test document.

source: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO)
authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO)
text:
Patent basics presentation
Nicholas Jensen
Academy Supervisory Patent Examiner Trainer 
Office of Patent Training
March 1, 2024

Learning objectives
3
• Recall the three types of patents.
• Understand the features of a patent.
• List three differences between a patent 
and a trade secret.
• Determine the patent term of a 
continuation or divisional patent 
application

What is a patent?
4
• The right to exclude others from:
– making, using, selling, offering for sale, 
or importing the claimed invention
• Limited term
• Territorial: A U.S. patent provides protection only in 
the United States
– No worldwide patents

Why invention matters and
what this means to you
5
Patents can:
•
Promote innovation and help 
safeguard inventions
•
Help companies grow  
•
Benefit the community by making 
new goods and services available
•
Be licensed to others so that the 
invention can be more widely used

The patent bargain
6
•
Utility and design patents give the patent owner the right to 
exclude others from making, using, importing, or selling the 
invention for a limited time period.
•
A plant patent precludes others from asexually reproducing, 
selling, offering for sale, or using the patented plant or any 
of its parts in the United States or importing them into the 
United States.
•
The inventor must fully disclose the invention so the public 
can benefit from it and expand on it. 
35 U.S.C. § 112

Types of patents  
7
Design

Is the invention eligible for utility patent protection?
8
35 U.S.C. § 101
process
machine 
composition of matter
manufacture

Protections for plants
9
• Plant patents: asexually propagated plants 
except for edible tubers
• Utility patents: genes, traits, methods, 
plant parts, or varieties
• Plant variety protections:  seed, tuber, and 
asexually propagated plants (issued by 
Plant Variety Protection Office, USDA)

Anatomy of a patent
10
•
Abstract
–
A short summary of the invention.
•
Written description
–
How does it work? 
How is it made or used?
•
Drawings
–
What does it look like?
•
Claims
–
The claim(s) define(s) the legal 
boundaries of the invention, 
similar to a deed to a property.
Invention title
Inventor’s Name
Issue date
Filing date
Drawings
Abstract
Documents 
referenced by 
examiner or applicant
*Example only – not a real patent

Sample claim
11
Claim 1. A chair comprising:
– a seat, 
– a back support attached to 
the seat,
– support arms attached to the 
seat and back support, and
– a base comprising a plurality 
of legs attached to the seat.
*Example only – not a real patent

The path to a patent
12

The patent application roadmap 
Back and forth
with the USPTO
13

How long does a patent last?
14
Patent term adjustment – the 
20-year term may be adjusted
as a result of delays by the 
USPTO to examine the 
application
Patent term extension - the 
term may be further extended
as a result of the regulatory 
review process before a 
product can be commercially 
marketed
Patent term = up to 20 years 
from earliest filing date of 
non-provisional application

Three main options
15
Inventors have several options when they invent something:
•
Apply for a patent
•
Keep their invention as a trade secret
•
Disclose their invention without a patent application, which 
makes it public and therefore, prior art.  Examples of disclosure:
– Marketing and selling
– Sharing videos online
– Publishing
– Using the invention in public spaces

Let’s talk Trade Secrets!

What is a trade secret?
17
• A trade secret is information that: 
– Has actual or potential independent economic 
value because it is generally unknown to others 
– Is valuable to others who can’t legitimately 
obtain the information, and 
– Is maintained as secret through reasonable 
efforts taken by the trade secret owner.

What is a trade secret?
18
• A trade secret can be formulas or recipes, 
product designs, customer lists, pricing 
schedules, manufacturing techniques, and 
marketing strategies.

Why use a trade secret?
19
Trade secret basics:
–
Protect commercially valuable proprietary information, e.g., formulas or 
business information that gives a competitive advantage
–
Trade secrets are not generally known and must be subject to reasonable 
efforts to preserve confidentiality
Common ways to lose a trade secret: 
–
Failure to take adequate steps to prevent disclosure
–
Owner or owner-authorized disclosure
–
Reverse engineering
–
Independent development

Trade secret examples
20
Some famous products are or were subject to claims of trade secret protection: 
•
Coca-Cola  
•
WD-40 
•
Kentucky Fried Chicken 
•
Lena Blackburne Rubbing Mud
•
Twinkies
•
New York Times Best Sellers list
Some of the claimed trade secrets at the hearts of these products have been 
secret for a long time, demonstrating the long-term benefits trade secret 
protection can provide owners who vigilantly guard their trade secrets.

Patents vs trade secrets
21
Patents
•
Information is published and, after 
expiration of the patent term, is in 
the public domain
•
Require an application process, 
which will not always result in a 
granted patent
•
A key remedy for violation of patent 
rights is a suit for patent 
infringement
Trade secrets
•
Can remain a secret indefinitely
•
Do not require filing of an 
application
•
A key remedy for violations of trade 
secret rights is a suit for 
misappropriation of trade secrets

Let’s talk about patents

Patent disclosure
23
• A patent application can disclose multiple 
inventions but only one will be examined 
per application.
• Continuing or divisional patent 
applications may be used to claim 
additional features or inventions disclosed 
in the earlier application.

Multiple inventions per product
24
A product
can be 
covered by 
more than 
one patent.
Original application
Disclosure

ingredient

Important fact
Continuation applications

protection on an 
invention

Continuing and divisional applications
26
•
A continuation application is an application for the invention(s) 
disclosed in a prior-filed co-pending application
•
The disclosure presented in the continuation must not include 
any new subject matter
•
Patents on continuation and divisional applications do not extend 
the term of patent protection of an invention (both patents expire 
20 years from the earliest filing date)

Later-filed applications
27
Later-filed continuation or divisional applications (“child” 
application) may claim the benefit of earlier application 
(“parent” application) if the parent application is still 
pending

Continuum of innovation
28
Example: addition of a coffee grinder to a coffee machine
Later-filed patent applications that are new and non-
obvious over previously patented inventions, and area not a 
continuation or divisional of a previously filed application, 
could lead to a new patent term.
Later improvements on a 
patented invention may be 
entitled to a new patent

Thank you!
www.uspto.gov

Nicholas Jensen
Academy Supervisory

keywords: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO)

title: Patents Act 1977 — Section 1
text: A patent may be granted only for an invention that is new, involves an inventive step, is capable of industrial application, and is not excluded by the Act.

title: Patents Act 1977 — Section 2
text: An invention is new if it does not form part of the state of the art. The state of the art includes matter made available to the public before the priority date.

title: Patents Act 1977 — Section 3
text: An invention involves an inventive step if it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art, having regard to the relevant state of the art.

title: Patents Act 1977 — Section 4
text: An invention is capable of industrial application if it can be made or used in any kind of industry, including agriculture.

title: Trade Marks Act 1994 — Section 1
text: A trade mark is a sign capable of being represented in the register and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings.

title: 35 U.S.C. § 101 — Inventions Patentable
text: A person who invents or discovers a new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or a new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent subject to the requirements of the patent laws.

title: 35 U.S.C. § 102 — Novelty
text: A claimed invention is not entitled to a patent when the relevant invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date, subject to statutory exceptions.

title: 35 U.S.C. § 103 — Non-Obvious Subject Matter
text: A patent may not be obtained when the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art would have made the invention obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
keywords: person having ordinary skill in the art

title: 35 U.S.C. § 112 — Specification
text: The specification must contain a written description of the invention and explain how to make and use it in clear and sufficient terms, and the specification must conclude with one or more claims defining the invention.

title: Patent Cooperation Treaty — System Overview
text: The PCT system allows an applicant to file one international patent application that has the same legal effect as filing separate national applications in PCT Contracting States, followed by international search and other international-phase procedures.

title: PCT — International Search
text: During the international phase, an international search is carried out and results in an international search report and a written opinion relating to the patentability of the claimed invention.

title: PCT — National Phase
text: After the international phase, the applicant may decide in which countries the application should proceed to the national phase, where the relevant national Offices determine whether a patent can be granted.

title: Traditional Drugs — Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani
text: CDSCO explains that Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drugs are medicines intended for internal or external use for diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder and manufactured according to the authoritative books specified in the legal framework.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 — Manufacture of Ayurvedic Drugs
text: The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 contain provisions governing the manufacture for sale of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs, including requirements associated with licensing and manufacturing premises.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 — Labelling and Packaging of Ayurvedic Drugs
text: The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 contain provisions concerning labelling, packing and specified requirements for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 — Licensing of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Drugs
text: Rule 158B sets out categories and licensing-related requirements for Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani medicines, including requirements concerning safety studies and evidence of effectiveness for specified categories.

source: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA)
title: Traditional Herbal Medicines
text: The UK has a traditional herbal registration route for certain herbal medicinal products. The route is intended for products with an established traditional use and requires compliance with applicable quality, safety and registration requirements.

title: Food Supplements, Nutrition and Health Claims
text: Food supplements sold in the UK are subject to food-labelling and health-claim requirements. A food product cannot claim or imply that it can treat, prevent or cure a disease or medical condition.

title: Dietary Supplements — Regulatory Overview
text: Dietary supplements are regulated under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and related FDA requirements. Applicable requirements include provisions concerning product composition, manufacturing, labelling and claims.

title: Label Claims for Food and Dietary Supplements
section: Health, Nutrient Content and Structure/Function Claims
text: FDA recognizes health claims, nutrient content claims and structure/function claims for foods and dietary supplements. Different regulatory requirements apply to each category of claim.

title: Structure/Function Claims for Dietary Supplements
text: Structure/function claims describe the role of a nutrient or dietary ingredient in affecting the normal structure or function of the human body. Certain such claims are subject to specific labelling and notification requirements.

title: Traditional Knowledge and Intellectual Property
text: WIPO provides resources on intellectual property and traditional knowledge, including traditional medical knowledge, protection approaches, access and benefit-sharing, and disclosure issues.

title: Traditional Knowledge and Genetic Resources Databases
text: WIPO maintains information about databases and registries of traditional knowledge and genetic resources maintained by member states and other organizations.

title: Madrid System — International Trademark Protection
text: The Madrid System provides a centralized system for filing and managing international trademark registrations. National or regional intellectual property offices decide whether protection can be granted in each designated territory under applicable law.
